newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Celuloza offer priced at discount - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Polish Celuloza offer priced at discount - analyst.

text.p: The public offering of Poland's Celuloza Swiecie SA paper firm is seen priced at a 40-70 percent discount to leading international paper companies and Warsaw bourse's top industrials, IB Austria said in a report.

The state treasury is offering 7.5 million Swiecie shares or 15 percent of the company on public subscription on April 15-18 at a minimum price of 15 zlotys and the strike price will be set at a special bourse session on April 22.

Remigiusz Tarka, IB Austria Securities analyst said in the report that given the minimum price and 1997 net profit forecast of 96.5 million zlotys Celuloza was priced 56 percent lower than other leading Warsaw industrial stocks.
It also represented a 46-63 percent discount to European and North American paper producers, he said.
Tarka said an expected upturn in world pulp and paper markets next year combined with expected strong growth of the domestic market bode well for Celuloza's 1998 performance.
"Investors can expect only a moderate earnings rise in 1997 but forecasts for 1998 are outstanding," he said in a report.
IB Austria predicts Celuloza's net earnings to almost double in 1998 to 184.5 million zlotys.

He said, however, that because of the heavily cyclical nature of the paper business financial investors might be wary of risks stemming from Celuloza's high exposure to highly volatile world cellulose markets.
"But with most major Polish firms already controlled by international paper firms, this is the last opportunity for investors to get into this market," he added.

Tarka said Celuloza, Central and Eastern Europe's biggest paper firm, with an annual output of 423,000 tonnes and a 27 percent share of the Polish market in terms of sales, was the country's most versatile producer.
Tarka said the broad range of products allowed Celuloza to show profits last year, when a deep slump in paper prices, pushed most world producers into the red.

But he said the firm's strategy and focus might change once a strategic investor is brought on board. The ministry plans to sell 65 percent of Celuloza and is now in talks with prospective investors. So far only Austria's Frantschach openly expressed interest in the firm.
